source.title: Sparse Training from Random Initialization: Aligning Lottery Ticket Masks using Weight Symmetry
source.authors: Mohammed Adnan; Rohan Jain; Ekansh Sharma; Rahul G. Krishnan; Yani Ioannou

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether permutation-based activation matching aligns independently initialized models by measuring loss barriers after alignment, a different measure from representation-distance similarity.
record.gate_note: The paper reports loss-barrier results for activation-matched models, which bear on V4's claim about mapping between models. Its sparse-training accuracy and ensemble-diversity results concern mask transfer and are not rows for the listed representation-convergence versions. It does not report direct representation-distance similarity, cross-modal alignment, shared-feature measurements, or universal features.
record.test_reason: The paper uses activation-based permutation matching (Git Re-Basin/REPAIR) as a tool to transfer lottery-ticket masks to new initializations. Its main results are the sparse-training accuracy and ensemble diversity of its own method. Figure 3's loss-barrier sweep is a check of the tool, shown only as a figure with no numbers. It measures weight-space linear mode connectivity, not how similar or mappable representations are, so it bears on no version directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that misalignment between the LTH mask and the new initialization's basin explains why masks fail to transfer. Permuting the mask improves sparse-training accuracy over the naive mask, and gives more functionally diverse solutions, on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet. Wider models are matched better, and the ImageNet gap stays larger.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation matching to obtain a neuron permutation and evaluates loss barriers and sparse-mask transfer, rather than measuring similarity of representations or distances between data points.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss barrier decreases as model width increases; the ImageNet barrier remains more prominent, which the authors associate with greedy matching and matching on a small subset of training data.

fits_no_version.finding: After activation-based permutation matching plus REPAIR, the interpolation loss barrier between independently initialized ResNet20 models shrinks as width grows (CIFAR-10/100). The barrier stays more prominent for ResNet50 on ImageNet, which the authors attribute to greedy matching on a small data subset. Figure only; no numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear mode connectivity modulo permutation between independently trained same-architecture networks improves with width.

record.code_released: not stated; the text says the codebase is publicly available but supplies no URL.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), as stated in the supplied metadata.
record.problems: The matching algorithm is described as greedy/approximate, and the ImageNet matching uses only a small subset of training data. The relevant loss-barrier results are presented in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Sparse-training accuracy tables and ensemble-diversity results were omitted because they measure mask-transfer performance or output diversity, not the representation mapping named by the tested version.

untested.parts: No comparison across architectures, objectives or data; no scale–alignment relation measured on representations.
No measure of shared features or subspaces across seeds. Permutation matching is used only as a tool, and only loss barriers are reported.
No measure of representation-mapping loss, stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping. Only weight-interpolation barriers are shown, as a tool check.
No interpretable features or circuits are compared across models.
No comparison of similarity metrics or of distribution shift.
No analysis of plateaus or of causes of alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Treated as T4: alignment is a means to mask transfer. The paper also cites Li et al. 2015 (an original source) for activation matching. Even if Figure 3 were credited to V3/V4, it is figure-only weight-space LMC evidence of the kind already established by Ainsworth et al. and Jordan et al.

versions.untested_parts: Scale-related alignment across different architectures, objectives, data, or modalities, and increasing capability.
Vision-language alignment on paired images and captions as model performance improves.
Shared features or subspaces across seeds are not measured; permutation-based basin alignment is not a direct feature-sharing measure.
Tests permutation matching and loss barriers, not stitching, relative representations, unpaired-data mapping, or direct task-performance loss from transferring representations.
Recurring interpretable features or circuits are not investigated.
Does not compare similarity measures, their settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment, or whether representational alignment plateaus.

relation.reason: The study uses neuron alignment to transfer lottery-ticket masks and evaluates sparse-training performance, functional diversity and weight-space connectivity.

tranche.reason: Activation matching and REPAIR serve sparse-mask transfer. The loss-barrier sweep checks matching quality; it does not measure shared features, representation similarity or interchangeability of representations.

source_check.notes: Figure 3 includes REPAIR after activation matching; its ImageNet width comparison uses w=1,2. The mask–basin explanation is an empirically supported hypothesis, rather than an established exclusive cause.
